segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What would "I know" be if it follows our rules?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it's an exception, s-e, "sé". You might have heard "lo sé, lo sé",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: literally "I know it", because "sé" by itself is a bit short, so you you often hear people saying "lo sé, lo sé", "I know it", rather than "sé, sé, sé".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is irregular, very irregular, s-e, no?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But the rest of the versions of saber are regular.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "he knows" or "she knows" or "it knows" or "you formal know"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that "quiero" was "I want", and "quiero" actually is an -er verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "I don't know what he wants"? What is "what"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Firstly you're not using the word for "he", you're just saying "he wants", and that's contained in the verb,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We didn't learn yet the word for "he", on purpose actually. We haven't been learning these words so that we can just use the verb for now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So try again: "I don't know what he wants."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You must feel comfortable with two words becoming one, ah? "I don't know what he wants", "No sé qué quiere." Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "he" is "él", él, e-l.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, if you want to be emphatic, "I don't know what *he* wants", or if you want to show or clarify who you're talking about, you can add that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you do that? "I don't know what he wants."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "No sé qué él quiere." Or you can say "No sé qué quiere él."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You can do either. One sounds more emphatic than the other, and this is much better understood in life practice, because the emphasis is not just in the sentence, it's with the hands, and the facial expression, and tone of voice, so it's something much better to get live.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "No sé qué él quiere", "No sé qué quiere él".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is the word for "her" first? We want to differentiate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is the word for "her", like in "I want to see her"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I want to see, to view, her"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you want to say "she sees", it's not "her", "I want to see her", it's "she".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And the word for "she" is "ella", ella.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now this is spelt e-l-l-a. Double L in Spanish is pronounced y, "ella".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you want to say "she sees" -

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: to see is "ver". What type of verb is it? -ar verb, -ir verb, -er verb?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: An -er verb. It seemed too obvious to ask.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sorry. (laughs) I thought you might have been asking for something more complicated.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No. This is an -er verb. So how do I say "she sees"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ella ve. And if I know who I'm talking about, I can just say "ve".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Maybe, when we are contrasting in the sentence we have a special desire to use these words.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: When I say contrasting, I mean in the sense maybe I say: "I want to invite him, but *she* doesn't want to invite him."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So even if we know who I'm talking about, there I will probably use the word for "she", because I'm making that contrast.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Again these are things you just do very naturally without realizing it, once you get practicing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Also because your native language probably does the same thing as well, even if you don't have the choice whether or not to put "she", like in English you always put it, you will stress it with your voice:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I don't want to invite him, but *she* does."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So because you are stressing that with your voice in English, that's also going to carry over. Many things are going to carry over that are positive language transfer that we might not necessarily address specifically.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say that: "I don't want to invite him, but she does want to invite him." So, "I don't want"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "She does" - so actually, we can just say "but she yes". What was the word for "yes"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sí. So we can just say "but she yes". How would you do that?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "No quiero invitarlo, pero ella sí." Or maybe I even use the word for "I" there to be emphatic:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Yo no quiero invitarlo." Yo, y-o. "Yo no quiero invitarlo, pero ella sí."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we said that "salir" was to leave or to go out.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now "I leave" or "I go out" is "salgo".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's irregular. Has the "g" sound popping up, "salgo".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But the rest of the versions are regular, so let's make them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you say "he goes out" or "he leaves" or "it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Again you're making some Turkish vowel harmony here, huh? (laughs)

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So that "sele" you put before is because it just sounds better. The mind has some kind of desire for this vowel harmony. It's very interesting. Sale.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now you can make me the rest. "They" or "you plural", "you guys"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if you want to say "I'm going out to eat", how is "I'm going out" again?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it should be "salo", but it was -

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salgo. So the irregularity is the same as the other one that we saw: "tener" - "tengo", "to have" - "I have", "venir" - "vengo", "to come" - "I come", "salir" - "salgo".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how do you say "I'm going out to eat"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is the verb. The verb is "to leave" or "to go out". So you don't need the word for "out".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Why did you think of the "a"? I think you felt it, no? You felt that that sense of movement, good!

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So "salgo a comer", it's a verb of movement, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Voy a comer", "I'm going to eat", "Salgo a comer", "I'm going out to eat", very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If we add on "que" to "tengo", and there's not really any comfortable translation for this,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but if we add on "que", we get "I have to", in the sense of "must", "have to".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for example, if you say "tengo que comer", we get "I have to eat".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we change the meaning of "tengo", like "have" which is just possession, to "have to" by adding "que".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And like I said, there's no comfortable translation. "Que" is "what" or "that", it's also used as "that" and we're going to use it like this later,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but again it's still it's still very uncomfortable to translate. So we would just say we add "que" and we get the meaning of "have to".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "I have to do it"? What was "to do"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hacer. So "I have to do it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Tengo que hacerlo", "Lo tengo que hacer", you have the option.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we've seen a few verbs with this "-go" business: "vengo", "I'm coming", "tengo", "I have", "salgo", "I leave",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and we've seen that the "-go" just pops up for the "I" version, doesn't pop up for the other versions, this G.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tienen. And how would you say "you have", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tienes, good. So if I give you the version for "he comes", it's "viene".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "you come"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's the English that's confusing you.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. So don't let that English "are you coming" confuse you. There's a lot we're doing in English there that we don't need to worry about for Spanish. "¿Cuándo vienes?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "A comer", very nice. "¿Cuándo vienes a comer?" "When are you coming to eat?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But I need you to be more specific. I'm giving you more information than just "have".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He, it, she, or formal you.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I want to know what you have... I want to know what you have?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What you have, or she, or it, very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that a very interesting detail about "tener" is that you can also translate it as "-tain", when this "-tain" forms part of another verb in English. So "contain" becomes "contener",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how was "it has", or "she has", "he has"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, we saw that it was "tiene". We haven't looked at why yet, but we've seen that it's a little bit irregular. In Spanish you can generalize this irregularity.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Obtengo. Sounds rather formal in English, but in Spanish you might use it like "get". "I get it",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That means "to put". And "I put", you have the same business with this G popping up, so how do you think it sounds: "I put"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And "poner" is interesting like "tener", because when we have "-pose" inside of a verb in English, we can turn that "-pose" into "poner" and we get the verb in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the example would be "compose" becomes "componer".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And how do you think you would say "I suppose"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We want to generalize our irregularities in Spanish. So how was "I put"? How was that, "I put"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you will hear: "Supongo que sí", "I suppose that yes". I said that "que" can also mean "that". "I suppose so", we say in English; in Spanish you say "I suppose that yes", "Supongo que sí". You will hear that.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we had "componer", to compose, "suponer", to suppose. How would you say "to impose"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo. And we said we can add on "que" to get the meaning of "have to".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you want to say "I have to see her", how would you say it: "I have to see her"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We could say "La tengo que ver" or "Tengo que verla", both are fine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I must see her, I owe to see her"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Debo verla." Or where else could you put that "la"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The difference between "tengo que" and "debo" is exactly like in English: we use "must" when it's a bit more serious, no? "I must see her", and we say "have to" like an everyday kind of thing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The way you use it in English and Spanish is exactly the same. So "debo" is a little bit more severe, a little bit more serious, and "tener que",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "to have to" with "que", is more everyday.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Tengo que comer ahora." What does that mean? "Tengo que comer ahora."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What does it mean if I say:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Voy a intentar comer más tarde. Voy a intentar comer más tarde."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Intentar? Can you say the whole sentence again?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It sounds odd, because it sounds like "I'm going with the intention to eat later."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, but it's not a noun, it's not "the intention", it's not "la intención", it's "intentar",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and when you hear that -r on the end you can suspect that it's a verb, most of the time it's going to be.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I'm going to try to eat later.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. "I'm going to try to eat later." Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's make a very short recap on these useful verbs that tend to have verbs coming after them in this way, like "voy a".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have "voy a", "I'm going to".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It might help to know that the word "power" is related to this word in Spanish. Of course when you can, when you're able to, you have the power to. So it's related and it begins with P: "I can".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So these verbs, "quiero", "voy a", "tengo que", "puedo", "debo", they're very useful, because we can just put the "to" form after.
